description:
In this video we will explore the controversy surrounding Diljit Dosanjh’s film Satluj, earlier titled Punjab 95. We will explain why the film disappeared from Zee5 in India, why the CBFC reportedly demanded several changes, and why the movie has created such a strong political and social debate. We will also examine the life of Jaswant Singh Khalra, his investigation into alleged illegal cremations, his abduction and murder, and the questions surrounding his political views.

We will also look at the violent history of the Punjab insurgency, including attacks on Hindu and Sikh civilians, police officers, journalists and political leaders. The video explains the role of Khalistani groups, Pakistan’s alleged support, the actions of Punjab Police and the controversial counterinsurgency strategy of KPS Gill. Finally, we will discuss whether banning films is the right solution, or whether biased narratives should be challenged by making better, more complete and historically accurate films.

Though I agree that the movie Satluj should ideally not be banned, I also understand why the Government may be reluctant to lift the ban.
The issue is not merely about one film. If every side starts producing counter-narratives exposing the other, it could reopen painful chapters of Punjab's past. I do not wish to revisit or highlight the atrocities committed against Hindus or any other community, because doing so may only deepen old wounds instead of healing them.
The Government appears to be trying to prevent the reopening of a sensitive internal fault line. India is already dealing with major security challenges on fronts like Jammu & Kashmir, and it would not want another emotionally charged issue to resurface in Punjab. The priority is to preserve social harmony and ensure that no misunderstanding develops between Sikhs and Hindus, who have lived together as one family for generations.
Therefore, the reluctance to lift the ban may be less about suppressing history and more about preventing a cycle of accusations and counter-accusations that could spread bitterness and disturb communal harmony.

Sutlej is a focused biopic about Jaswant Singh Khalra, not a 10-hour historical documentary about the entire 80s and 90s Punjab insurgency. 1. Initial political situation: Before the controversy, AAP is considered the strongest electoral force in Punjab. The BJP has a comparatively smaller base, while the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) has lost some of its traditional Sikh support, and Congress retains a mixed voter base.


2. A sensitive issue emerges: A film based on a controversial period of Punjab's history becomes the center of public attention. Instead of remaining only an entertainment release, it starts generating political and emotional debate.


3. Restriction creates more attention: The film is restricted or removed from a platform. Rather than reducing interest, the controversy itself becomes the news. Media coverage, social media discussions, and public curiosity increase dramatically. Many people who might never have watched the film now actively seek it out. This reflects the idea that attempts to suppress something can sometimes make it more widely discussed.


4. Historical memories return to public debate: The film and the controversy revive discussions about the militancy era, Khalistan, counter-insurgency, human rights, and security. Political discourse shifts away from everyday issues such as development, jobs, education, and governance toward identity and historical grievances.


5. Different communities react differently: People interpret the controversy through different personal, political, and historical perspectives. Instead of a common political narrative, public opinion becomes more polarized.


6. Possible impact on Hindu voters: If security becomes the dominant issue, some Hindu voters who were considering AAP may conclude that the BJP is stronger on law-and-order or national security issues and shift their support accordingly.


7. Possible impact on Sikh voters: At the same time, some Sikh voters who had previously supported AAP may feel that identity-related issues have become more important and return to traditional Sikh political parties such as the Shiromani Akali Dal. Others may remain with AAP or support Congress, so the shift would not necessarily be universal.


8. AAP's vote share declines: Because AAP draws support from multiple communities, even moderate losses from both Hindu and Sikh voters could reduce its overall vote share more than that of other parties.


9. Fragmented election outcome: Instead of one party securing a clear majority, the election could become more fragmented. BJP may increase its share among Hindu voters, SAD may recover part of its traditional Sikh base, Congress could retain a mixed section of voters, and AAP could lose enough support to fall short of a majority.


10. Strategic objective : Under this theory, the goal would not necessarily be for the BJP to win a majority on its own. Rather, it would be to weaken AAP's broad coalition, increase political polarization around identity issues, and create a more divided electoral landscape where no single rival dominates.

The movie is grounded in official court documents and focuses on the real story of Jaswant Khalra — how he uncovered unclaimed bodies and was killed by the police. That part is factually accurate.
I understand the criticism that it doesn’t show the militants’ wrongdoings or Hindus who were killed. That’s fair. At the same time, The Kashmir Files also centered on the suffering of Kashmiri Pandits without covering every angle of Muslim suffering — which made sense for its focus. This film does the same by highlighting the tragedy of many innocent Punjabi Sikh youth who died in fake encounters. The 2,097 documented cases were from Amritsar alone, so the broader estimate for Punjab during the height of militancy isn’t unreasonable.
Many Punjabis who lived through that period say the movie reflects what they saw. The main valid point is that it doesn’t address militants targeting Hindus, but the film’s clear purpose was to bring attention to the largely overlooked suffering of Sikh civilians — similar to how Kashmir Files spotlighted the Pandits.
It’s not promoting Khalistan. It has a 9.6/10 on IMDb for a reason. I’d encourage everyone to watch it with an open mind and form their own opinion. Disagreement over calling Bhindranwale a “Sant” shouldn’t overshadow the documented events shown here.
